items.title: Glenn Close cries! John Malkovich weeps! But it’s Nathan Fielder everyone wants to talk to at the honorary Oscars
items.summary:
All of Hollywood’s biggest stars are in attendance for the Governors’ awards, but nobody gets drunk and the biggest draw is an awkward documentarian

Timothée Chalamet was seconds away from getting into trouble. It was just after 6pm in Hollywood and Lynette Howell Taylor, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, was trying to corral a crowd of 700-odd people into sitting down so she could begin the Governors awards ceremony. She jokingly threatened to start calling out anyone still standing by name if they didn’t sit down imminently. Chalamet was the only one left on his feet, circling the table where he was due to sit next to his girlfriend, Kylie Jenner, opposite Tom Holland and Zendaya. Howell Taylor gave him a few seconds’ grace. He looked like the popular kid testing how far he could push a headteacher.

The Governors awards had a curiously school-like atmosphere this year. Even the carpet in the Ray Dolby Ballroom was faded and striped. The social structure was much the same: closed-off and insular, with cliques, alliances, legendary enmities and intricate hierarchies of popularity and influence. There were those who seemed entirely comfortable – Chalamet, Holland, Tom Cruise, Matt Damon, Willem Dafoe, Seth Rogen – and others still angling for a better table.

Continue reading...

items.title: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw
items.summary:
Pattinson is a character actor whose talent for inscrutable appraisal may mean a new era for 007. Will this more willowy, classy Bond leave sexism in the shadows?

• New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
• Share your thoughts on the casting
• Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to James Bond

If it wasn’t Bond … maybe it would have been Dr No in some hi-tech reboot. But Robert Pattinson – with his movie-star chops and track record in hip A24-type character turns, and his gift for cool, inscrutable appraisal and sensual menace – is an exquisite choice as 007, playing on the darker and more sophisticated notes of Pattinson’s performing personality.

And let’s hope, incidentally, that the actor now isn’t forced into a five-hour daily gym regimen to bulk up. I like the taller and more willowy Bond that Pattinson represents, the Bond from whose frame the tux hangs gracefully, the Bond with elegant abandon who’s a former British Naval officer, not a former US Navy Seal, the Bond who with a crinkly-eyed reptilian grin can style out waking up with a hangover after too many whisky-and-sodas at the baccarat table.
items.t: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw

items.title: Filipiñana review – sexual exploitation at the golf club in menacing satire on class and privilege
items.summary:
A sense of threat permeates a verdant private golf course in water-deprived Manila, peopled with submissive tee-girls and geisha-style caddies catering to the male clientele

A spectacle filled with dreamlike tableaux, off-centre framing and slow trance-like zooms, Filipiñana is an elegant and politically pointed feature debut from the Filipino director and London Film School graduate Rafael Manuel, developed from his award-winning short film of the same name. It is a melancholy satire on caste shame, sexual politics and land exploitation in the Philippines, symbolised by a private golf course in Manila, an artificial landscape as depthless and surreal as the gardens in Last Year in Marienbad. Irrigating the vivid greens and undulating fairways requires oceans of precious water – water that, in the course of one unbearable heatwave, is rationed for the sweating lower orders in the city, way beyond the golf club’s luxurious precincts.

Jorrybell Agoto plays the “Filipiñana” of the title, 17-year-old Isabel, the inscrutable witness to the club’s occult traditions and one of its legion of demurely submissive uniformed “tee-girls”, whose sole purpose is to position the balls for the wealthy (male) golfers about to tee off. (This is a task subject to much giggling innuendo in private among the girls themselves.) The tee-girls are not allowed to step on the course itself; that is the prerogative of the caddies, all women, each quaintly dressed in uniforms like that of an airline…
items.t: Filipiñana review – sexual exploitation at the golf club in menacing satire on class and privilege

items.title: The Nice Ones review – invasion of the sunny personality snatchers
items.summary:
Peter Stylianou’s watchably unsettling tale of unbalanced minds and Unidentified Aerial Phenomena does its best to please

Drone shots are two-a-penny in cinema these days, but it’s a mark of this £80,000 British indie sci-fi’s visual astuteness that it largely avoids them in a film plagued by drone-like entities. Instead, it takes a suggestive approach: protagonist Kate (Joelle Rae) is staring out of the window on a car journey, up into the night sky, when a pinprick of light flares out before shooting out a laser towards the ground – then darting off into a cloudbank.

Kate chews over this anomaly with boyfriend Dale (Emrhys Cooper), en route to a get-together of his old uni gang in a countryside Airbnb. Already not at ease among his mates, Kate gets a ribbing when she repeats her UFO story (or Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, as they are called these days). And there are knowing glances about her psychiatric history: she once fended off an abusive boyfriend at knifepoint, insisting he was possessed. But if she is delusional, then it seems to be spreading: her one ally, spacey teacher Shelly (Ayvianna Snow), re-enters the room after a suspiciously long fag break, marvelling about how they will all imminently join “the light”.

Continue reading...
items.t: The Nice Ones review – invasion of the sunny personality snatchers

items.title: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
items.summary:
The latest in our series of writers picking their most comforting rewatches is a tribute to Curtis Hanson’s insightful 2000 comedy drama

I’m allergic to movies and books about writers. Washed-up novelists, aspiring screenwriters, creative writing professors in the throes of a midlife crisis who cheat on their wives – take your pick. Chalk it up to my being a writer who for two decades wrote continually and fruitlessly about writers. And yet, I love Wonder Boys, Curtis Hanson’s 2000 comedy drama about a rumpled creative writing professor who can’t seem to finish his second novel and is having an affair with his boss’s wife. It’s partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all.

I saw Wonder Boys on its opening weekend, when I was 17, and the notion of poring over novels with kindred spirits in a sun-dappled seminar room at some leafy liberal arts college – where I’d find myself a year later – held endless appeal. Even the misadventures of the film’s professor, Grady Tripp (Michael Douglas, never better), seemed romantic to me. On the eve of his university’s annual literary festival, Grady’s wife leaves him. His lover, Sara, announces she’s pregnant with his child. And James Leer, his brilliant but troubled student, who can rattle off Hollywood suicides in alphabetical order, shows up at the festival’s kick-off party cradling what may or may not be a cap gun. Grady responds to all this with the urgency of a veteran pot smoker – which he is.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie

items.title: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
items.summary:
The adventurous weirdness of the Gunn/Safran era that fans responded to is now history. Can the DCU ever get back on track?

What was Warner Bros’ plan in 2022, when the studio decided to reboot its superhero output, jettison the increasingly muddled DC Extended Universe (DCEU) and replace it with a sparkling new DC Universe (DCU)? In part it was to wipe the slate clean after years of false starts, abandoned storylines and tonal lurches. There was a little bit of Marvel envy to proceedings, and quite possibly a desire to avoid having to ever again discuss Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice’s numerous failings. But mostly it was to take advantage of hiring of a man whom nobody could accuse of being short of ideas on how to make comic book movies. To a greater or lesser extent, the plan was James Gunn.

Fast forward four years, and that plan lies in tatters. Gunn and his fellow DC Studios CEO Peter Safran have this week been fired (though they will reportedly stay on as film-makers), and Jeremy Latcham, another former Marvel man, is the new boss. What is the plan now? Nobody seems to know, and there is not much point asking David Ellison, the man whose Skydance empire has now gobbled up two of the former big five Hollywood studios (Paramount last year and Warner…

items.title: ‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong
items.summary:
As Amazon MGM Studios prepares to announce the next 007, much rides on how the news is broken. From double bookings to health and safety embarrassments, we look back at how not to do it

And then there were five. While nothing has been officially announced, it is widely understood that the shortlist to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond is now down to a handful of actors: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult.

The hunt for a new Bond comes at a propitious moment for the franchise as a whole, 25 films in (not counting the two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983). After Daniel Craig stood down from the role after completing No Time to Die (in which Bond appeared to be killed in a missile strike), Amazon MGM Studios paid over $1bn to acquire “creative control” from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the British-American heirs to the series’ original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.

items.title: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past
items.summary:
The latest film version of the Dickens classic A Christmas Carol is decent enough, though its star is rather better as the legendary miser before redemption arrives

Here for lovers of Dickens – and fans of subtext – is an unexpectedly watchable new movie version of A Christmas Carol starring a top-hatted and heavily madeup Johnny Depp; it is a film about whether it’s possible for a man to earn redemption before it is too late. (The answer is … sure, as long as you say sorry and change your ways. But Mr Scrooge never launched a libel action against the Sun for calling him an un-Christmassy old meanie.)

In fact, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern and director Ti West have put together a perfectly serviceable, faithful adaptation – a tradaptation, if you will – of Dickens’s masterpiece about the hideous old miser saved from damnation on Christmas Eve by the appearance of three Christmas ghosts, from yuletides past, present and future. It sticks to the accepted narrative beats and more or less all the familiar episodes, but with a few twists.

Continue reading...
items.t: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past

items.title: Victorian Psycho review – Maika Monroe has a blast in unsteady horror romp
items.summary:
The It Follows and Longlegs star tears into the role of a murderous governess in this hit-and-miss adaptation of Virginia Feito’s gory novel

It’s not that hard to figure out why a lower-class woman toiling away in Victorian England would be so easily driven to violently murder everyone around her. If it’s not the brittle entitlement of those who employ you, it’s the unending misogyny of the system you’re forced to be a subservient part of, all the while being underpaid and undervalued and at the mercy of sexual violence, a multitude of diseases and an average lifespan of just 42.

As Winifred Notty (Maika Monroe) fills the frame in Victorian Psycho, heading to a new job as governess for a rich family, it’s easy to be on her side. Even as her murderous impulses start to rear their head, they’re made somewhat understandable, although Winifred isn’t just a woman reacting to the various injustices of the time – she’s one responding to a demon within her, a darkness she has chosen to embrace rather than resist. Darkness is her friend, a protection against harm, and a way to possess some sort of control in a world that has denied her any of it.

Continue reading...
items.t: Victorian Psycho review – Maika Monroe has a blast in unsteady horror romp
